Therefore, the key enablers of FT economic viability are primarily (1) sourcing low- cost feedstocks for generating syngas, (2) operating at a large scale to maximize the benefits of economies of scale to minimize relative capital expenditure impacts, and (3) maximizing selectivity to SAF-range hydrocarbons and valorizing coproducts to offset costs. 2.1.1.2 Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids In 2011, a second pathway to SAF was approved: SPK from HEFA. HEFA is a mature TRL 9 pathway that currently represents the most widely commercialized and one of the lowest-cost SAF production routes in the United States (see Table 4) (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024b). Unlike FT, where small molecular building blocks (syngas) are combined to construct long-chain hydrocarbons, the HEFA process effectively works in reverse. The process starts from feedstocks comprising predominantly high-molecular-weight triglycerides and fatty acids (e.g., seed oils; animal fats, oils, and greases); HEFA deconstructs these large molecules into fuel-range hydrocarbons. Shown in Figure 10, the HEFA process involves four key stages: (1) pretreatment to remove solids and other contaminants that may impact catalyst operability and lifetime; (2) a hydrodeoxygenation step to remove oxygen and saturate C-H bonds; (3) partial isomerization of the product to generate branched hydrocarbons (e.g., iso-alkanes) with improved fuel handling properties (e.g., freeze point, viscosity); and (4) hydrocracking to break up the initial long-chain hydrocarbon into smaller fuel-range molecules (e.g., C –C for SAF). Steps 3 and 4 are 8 16 conducted at the same time using the same catalyst in the same reactor. Similar to the FT pathway, the HEFA process generates a distribution of hydrocarbon products including fuel gas (e.g., lights), naphtha (e.g., gasoline), diesel, and kerosene. The relative breakdown of each component is largely dictated by the operator and the applied processing steps. Specifically, with the starting HEFA feedstock already comprising diesel-range C -C 16 18 hydrocarbons, all that is needed is a deoxygenation and mild isomerization step to produce drop- in ready renewable diesel. However, to produce jet fuel in the range of C -C , a third 8 16 ‘hydrocracking and isomerization’ stage is required to reduce the carbon number and effectively break the molecules into smaller pieces. As the hydrocarbons are cracked, inevitably some carbon is lost to the formation of smaller molecules in the C -C range, reducing the overall 1 6 carbon yield to jet fuel. Currently, the higher yield and lower capital and operating costs associated with renewable diesel production has contributed to the majority of domestic HEFA operators favoring renewable diesel production over SAF. Production estimates for 2030 suggest approximately 80% of HEFA production capacity will be directed to renewable diesel (Rosales Calderon et al. 2024b). 13 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
